_export_meta.target_lesson_title: Life Factors — What Shapes Health Across the Lifespan
_export_meta.adaptation_notes: The Pearson BTEC Tech Award Component 3 free-tier build opens with 'factors affecting health and wellbeing' — broadly the same conceptual territory but with a shorter, six-category Pearson list (genetic, lifestyle, social, cultural, economic, environmental). This spec names THIRTEEN distinct life factors with detailed sub-bullets (e.g. seven types of abuse, four parenting styles, named conditions). Use BTEC as a tonal reference but rebuild the content list to match the spec's exact taxonomy. Reuse care-setting framing only.

source_lesson.title: Defining Health & Wellbeing + Physical Factors
source_lesson.description: What health and wellbeing really means, plus inherited conditions, physical and mental ill health.
source_lesson.content_html:
What Is Health and Wellbeing?

Many people think being “healthy” simply means not being ill. The Pearson BTEC specification uses a much broader definition. Health and wellbeing is a combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing — it is not just the absence of disease or illness. This means a person can be physically fit but still have poor wellbeing if they feel lonely, stressed, or unhappy.

Key Fact

Health and wellbeing is defined as a combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing, and not just the absence of disease or illness.

This definition matters because it shapes how health and social care professionals assess and support individuals. They do not just treat physical symptoms — they consider a person’s mental state, relationships, and overall quality of life. Throughout this unit, you will see factors that affect health and wellbeing grouped into physical, lifestyle, social, cultural, economic, and environmental categories.

Inherited Conditions

Some health conditions are passed from parents to children through inherited conditions. These are caused by faulty genes and are present from birth, though symptoms may not appear immediately. The specification requires you to know two key examples.

Sickle cell disease affects the red blood cells, which become crescent-shaped instead of round. This means they can block blood vessels and do not carry oxygen as effectively. Symptoms include episodes of severe pain (called crises), fatigue, and increased risk of infections. It affects physical wellbeing through pain and tiredness, emotional wellbeing through frustration and anxiety about crises, and social wellbeing because hospital stays and absences from school or work can lead to isolation.

Cystic fibrosis causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system. This leads to frequent chest infections, difficulty breathing, and problems absorbing nutrients from food. Daily physiotherapy and medication are needed. The condition affects all areas of PIES development — physically through breathing difficulties, intellectually through missed education, emotionally through frustration at limitations, and socially through feeling different from peers.

Physical Ill Health

Physical ill health covers conditions that damage the body’s normal functions. The specification names three conditions you must know.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a general term for conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels, including coronary heart disease, heart attacks, and strokes. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, poor diet, and lack of exercise. CVD can limit a person’s physical abilities and create anxiety about future health events, reducing emotional wellbeing.

Obesity is when a person has an excessive amount of body fat, usually measured using BMI. A BMI of 30 or above is classified as obese. Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, joint problems, and some cancers. It can also affect emotional wellbeing through low self-esteem and social wellbeing through bullying or discrimination.

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body does not produce enough insulin or the body’s cells do not react to insulin properly. This leads to high blood sugar levels. It is strongly linked to obesity, poor diet, and lack of physical activity. If unmanaged, it can cause serious complications including nerve damage, kidney problems, and vision loss.

Key Fact

CVD, obesity, and type 2 diabetes are closely linked — they share common risk factors such as poor diet, lack of physical activity, and smoking. Obesity significantly increases the risk of developing both CVD and type 2 diabetes.

Mental Ill Health

Mental ill health affects how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. The two conditions named in the specification are anxiety and stress.

Anxiety involves persistent feelings of worry, fear, or nervousness that are difficult to control. Physical symptoms can include a racing heart, sweating, and difficulty sleeping. Anxiety can prevent a person from socialising, attending work or school, and enjoying daily activities — affecting all areas of their PIES development.

Stress is the body’s reaction to feeling threatened or under pressure. Short-term stress can be helpful (motivating someone before an exam), but long-term stress damages health. Chronic stress can cause headaches, high blood pressure, digestive problems, weakened immunity, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and withdrawal from relationships.

Physical Abilities and Sensory Impairments

Physical abilities refer to what a person can physically do — walking, lifting, gripping, and so on. Conditions like arthritis, cerebral palsy, or injuries from accidents can reduce physical abilities. This can affect independence, employment opportunities, and self-esteem.

Sensory impairments affect the senses, most commonly sight and hearing. A person who is deaf or blind faces challenges in communication, accessing information, and navigating their environment. Sensory impairments can lead to social isolation if support is not available, and may affect emotional wellbeing through frustration or dependency on others.

Both physical abilities and sensory impairments highlight why the definition of health and wellbeing goes beyond “absence of disease” — a person may have a stable condition but still experience reduced wellbeing if they lack support, face discrimination, or feel excluded from social activities.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: In the Component 3 exam, questions often use a case study about a named individual. When explaining how a physical factor affects health and wellbeing, always link your answer to all relevant areas of PIES (Physical, Intellectual, Emotional, Social). For example, if asked about the impact of obesity, explain the physical effects (joint pain, increased disease risk), then show how these lead to emotional effects (low self-esteem) and social effects (bullying, isolation). The best answers make chains of reasoning — one effect leading to another.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health and wellbeing is a combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing — not just the absence of disease or illness.
  • Inherited conditions (sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis), physical ill health (CVD, obesity, type 2 diabetes), and mental ill health (anxiety, stress) all affect multiple areas of PIES development.
  • Physical abilities and sensory impairments can reduce independence and social participation, showing why wellbeing is about more than just physical health.

practice_questions.text: Identify one inherited condition that can affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for one correct identification:
• Sickle cell disease (1)
• Cystic fibrosis (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two physical effects that a person with cystic fibrosis may experience.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct physical effect (max 2):
• Thick mucus builds up in the lungs (1)
• Frequent chest infections (1)
• Difficulty breathing (1)
• Problems absorbing nutrients from food (1)
• Need for daily physiotherapy (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how obesity can have a negative effect on an individual's emotional and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed explanation across emotional and social wellbeing:
• Obesity can cause low self-esteem (1) because the individual may feel unhappy with their appearance or physical abilities (1).
• Obesity can lead to social isolation (1) because the individual may experience bullying or discrimination from others, causing them to withdraw from social activities (1).
• Accept other valid chains linking obesity to emotional or social effects.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how mental ill health, such as anxiety, can affect an individual's health and wellbeing across all areas of PIES.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion covering multiple PIES areas with developed points.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points with little development.
Indicative content:
• Physical: racing heart, sweating, difficulty sleeping, weakened immune system
• Intellectual: difficulty concentrating, poor performance at school or work
• Emotional: persistent worry, low self-esteem, feeling unable to cope
• Social: avoiding social situations, withdrawing from friends and family, difficulty maintaining relationships
• Links between areas, e.g. poor sleep (physical) leading to difficulty concentrating (intellectual).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which inherited conditions have a greater impact on an individual's health and wellbeing than physical ill health conditions such as obesity or type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Inherited conditions:
• Present from birth — individual has no control
• Often lifelong with no cure (e.g. sickle cell, cystic fibrosis)
• Affect PIES from an early age — missed education, social isolation from childhood
• Daily treatment regimes can be exhausting and restrictive
Physical ill health:
• Often linked to lifestyle choices — some can be prevented or managed
• Obesity and type 2 diabetes can be improved with diet and exercise
• However, CVD can be fatal if not managed
• Social stigma around obesity can severely affect emotional wellbeing
Conclusion: Both have significant impacts but inherited conditions may be considered greater because the individual has no control and they are lifelong. However, the impact depends on the severity of the condition, the support available, and the individual's circumstances.

practice_questions.text: Amir is 45 years old. He was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. He works long hours in a stressful office job and rarely exercises. He has also been feeling anxious about his health. Using the case study, assess how Amir's physical factors are affecting his overall health and wellbeing. In your answer, consider the impact on his physical, intellectual, emotional, and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive, well-developed response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Amir's specific circumstances. Chains of reasoning throughout.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some developed links to the case study.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development or links to Amir.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure increase risk of CVD, stroke, kidney damage. Lack of exercise worsens both conditions. Fatigue and physical symptoms reduce his ability to function.
• Intellectual: Stress and anxiety can cause difficulty concentrating at work. High blood sugar levels can cause brain fog. This may affect his job performance.
• Emotional: Anxiety about his health creates persistent worry. He may feel guilty about his lifestyle. Low mood and fear about long-term complications. Stress from work compounds his emotional state.
• Social: Long working hours reduce time for socialising. Anxiety may cause him to withdraw from friends and family. He may avoid social events involving food or alcohol due to his diabetes.
• Links between factors: stress (mental ill health) raises blood pressure (physical ill health), creating a negative cycle. Lack of exercise worsens both diabetes and anxiety.
• Person-specific: At 45, Amir is in middle adulthood where health risks increase naturally. His stressful job is both a cause and an aggravating factor.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the correct definition of health and wellbeing?
options: The absence of disease or illness
Being physically fit and able to exercise
A combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing, not just the absence of disease
Having no inherited conditions or disabilities

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an inherited condition named in the specification?
Sickle cell disease causes red blood cells to become _____ shaped instead of round.
A BMI of _____ or above is classified as obese.
Match each condition to its correct description:
right: Conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels
The body does not produce enough insulin or cells do not react to it properly
Persistent feelings of worry, fear, or nervousness that are difficult to control
